Bug_Title: Use of the "@Async" annotation on methods declared within a "@Configuration" class in Spring Boot
Bug_Details:
@Configuration is a class-level annotation indicating that an object is a source of bean definitions. @Configuration classes declare beans through @Bean -annotated methods. Calls to @Bean methods on @Configuration classes can
also be used to define inter-bean dependencies. The @Bean annotation indicates that a method instantiates, configures, and initializes a
new object to be managed by the Spring IoC container.
Annotating a method of a bean with @Async will make it execute in a separate thread. In other words, the caller will not wait for the
completion of the called method.
The @Async annotation is not supported on methods declared within a @Configuration class. This is because @Async methods are typically used for asynchronous processing, and they require certain infrastructure to be set up, which may not be
available or appropriate in a @Configuration class.
Bug_Explanation: The @Async annotation is not supported on methods declared within a @Configuration class. This is because @Async methods are typically used for asynchronous processing, and they require certain infrastructure to be set up, which may not be available or appropriate in a @Configuration class.
Trigger_Explanation: The test case calls the method'showBug' which triggers the bug as it's a @Async method declared within a @Configuration class. The'showBug' method tries to access the bean 'context' from the ApplicationContext, which is not available in the context of the Configuration class, therefore it throws a NullPointerException.
Model_Explanation: The @Async annotation is used on the'showBug' method, which is a method within a @Configuration class. This is not allowed as per the Spring documentation. The @Async annotation is used to indicate that a method should be executed in a separate thread. However, @Configuration classes are typically used to declare beans, and they are not designed to support asynchronous execution. Therefore, using the @Async annotation on a method within a @Configuration class can lead to unexpected behavior or errors.
